Reinforcement learning on one page

The classical problems of reinforcement learning, in a teaching order, and the method that answers each one.

October 18, 202613 min read

Reinforcement learning, one idea at a timePart 0 of 5

This article is a tour of the classical ideas of reinforcement learning, in a teaching order: handing out credit, exploring, learning from your own guesses, and what goes wrong when you scale all of that up. Later articles take one method each and go deep.

Throughout, sss is a state, aaa an action, rrr the reward you get and s′s's′ the state you land in.

A state's value is an average of its actions' values

vπ(s)=∑aπ(a∣s) qπ(s,a)v_\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\, q_\pi(s,a) vπ​(s)=a∑​π(a∣s)qπ​(s,a)

For the best values, take the max in place of the average

v∗(s)=max⁡aq∗(s,a)π∗(s)=arg⁡max⁡aq∗(s,a)\begin{aligned} v_*(s) &= \max_a q_*(s,a) \\ \pi_*(s) &= \arg\max_a q_*(s,a) \end{aligned} v∗​(s)π∗​(s)​=amax​q∗​(s,a)=argamax​q∗​(s,a)​

Average over the actions the policy picks and you get the value of a state. Take the best action in place of the average and you get the best value.

Credit assignment

Credit assignment is one of the classic problems. You play a whole game and only learn at the end whether you won. Which actions deserve the credit? The simplest answer is to discount. If the reward arrives at step 6, step 5 gets γ\gammaγ times it, step 4 gets γ2\gamma^2γ2 times it, and so on. Adding up the discounted rewards from step ttt gives the return GtG_tGt​.

Gt=Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2Rt+3+⋯\begin{aligned} G_t = R_{t+1} &+ \gamma R_{t+2} \\ &+ \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \cdots \end{aligned} Gt​=Rt+1​​+γRt+2​+γ2Rt+3​+⋯​

A value function stores that number for each state, so a late reward reaches the earlier steps.

Explore or exploit: the bandit

The first reinforcement learning problem most people hear about is the multi-armed bandit. Imagine a casino with ten slot machines, each paying a hidden average plus noise. You have 1,000 pulls. The Q table is a single row, because there is one state, the casino, and ten actions. Q(a)Q(a)Q(a) is the average payout of machine aaa so far, and n(a)n(a)n(a) counts its pulls.

Q(a)←Q(a)+1n(a)(r−Q(a))Q(a) \leftarrow Q(a) + \tfrac{1}{n(a)}\bigl(r - Q(a)\bigr) Q(a)←Q(a)+n(a)1​(r−Q(a))

Ten slot machines, 1,000 pulls (ε = 0 is greedy, ε = 0.1 explores a little)
  1. Set Q(a) = 0 and n(a) = 0 for each machine a.
  2. Repeat for 1,000 pulls:
  3. With probability ε pick a random machine. Otherwise pick argmax Q(a), at random on a tie.
  4. Pull it and observe the payout r. Set n(a) = n(a) + 1.
  5. Q(a) ← Q(a) + (r − Q(a)) / n(a)

Always pulling the best-looking machine (greedy) locks onto its first good pick. Pulling a random one 1 time in 10 corrects the numbers.

Rule, 200 runs Share of the last 200 pulls on the best machine
Greedy, ε = 0 35.5%
Random pull 1 in 10, ε = 0.1 77.5%

Different ways to train the Q function

Most methods below train an action-value function: Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a) says how good action aaa is in state sss.

The loop every method here shares
  1. Pick an action a in the state s (greedy, or random with probability ε).
  2. Take it. Observe the reward r and the next state s′.
  3. Build a target for Q(s, a).
  4. Q(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α · (target − Q(s, a))
α is the step size. The methods differ in line 3.

Monte Carlo. Wait for the episode to end and use the real return. Nothing is guessed, but some games never end.

target=Gt\text{target} = G_t target=Gt​

Q-learning (part 1). Use the reward you just got plus your best guess for the next state. Updating a guess from another guess is called bootstrapping, and learning from the gap between two guesses is temporal difference (TD) learning. You learn at every step, but the table gets too big, random tries can send you off the cliff in part 1, and a max over noisy numbers runs high.

target=r+γmax⁡a′Q(s′,a′)\text{target} = r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a') target=r+γa′max​Q(s′,a′)

n-step TD (part 2). In between: add up nnn real rewards, then let a guess cover the rest. For action values, one common form is n-step Sarsa. Near the end of an episode fewer than nnn are left, so you use the real return you have.

target=Rt+1+⋯+γn−1Rt+n+γnQ(St+n,At+n)\text{target} = R_{t+1} + \dots + \gamma^{n-1}R_{t+n} + \gamma^n Q(S_{t+n}, A_{t+n}) target=Rt+1​+⋯+γn−1Rt+n​+γnQ(St+n​,At+n​)

Sarsa (part 4). The name lists State, Action, Reward, next State, next Action. It uses the action you actually take next, so it describes how you really behave, but one unlucky random action makes the target noisy.

target=r+γ Q(s′,a′)\text{target} = r + \gamma\, Q(s',a') target=r+γQ(s′,a′)

Expected Sarsa (part 4). It averages over every next action by its probability, which removes that noise. You need every probability.

target=r+γ∑a′π(a′∣s′) Q(s′,a′)\text{target} = r + \gamma \sum_{a'} \pi(a'\mid s')\,Q(s',a') target=r+γa′∑​π(a′∣s′)Q(s′,a′)

Double Q-learning. The max runs high because the best-looking action often has the luckiest noise. One table picks and a second scores, which reduces maximization bias. Each learns from half the updates.

target=r+γ Q2(s′,arg⁡max⁡a′Q1(s′,a′))\text{target} = r + \gamma\, Q_2\big(s', \arg\max_{a'} Q_1(s',a')\big) target=r+γQ2​(s′,arga′max​Q1​(s′,a′))

DQN (part 3). A neural network replaces the table so similar states share what they learn. Replay and a frozen copy reduce instability, but do not guarantee stability. Numbers still run high on some tasks, it needs many samples, and it handles only discrete actions.

The family tree

Here are the methods as a family tree to commit to memory. A line goes from a method to one that fixes a problem it has, and blue boxes get their own article. It is the tree from Breaking Bellman, a small game I made.

Top half. Trial and error leads to Monte Carlo, then Q-learning and n-step TD (parts 1 and 2).

Bottom half. Q-learning's problems lead to Sarsa, DQN and Double Q-learning (parts 3 to 5).

Where the Bellman equation comes from

The Bellman equation says the value of a state is the reward you get next plus the discounted value of the state you land in. That turns a return over the whole future into one step.

Bellman equation for a policy Eq. 3.14

vπ(s)=Eπ ⁣[Rt+1+γ vπ(St+1)∣St=s]v_\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\!\left[R_{t+1} + \gamma\, v_\pi(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s\right] vπ​(s)=Eπ​[Rt+1​+γvπ​(St+1​)∣St​=s]

Bellman optimality equation: the average becomes a max Eq. 3.20

q∗(s,a)=E[Rt+1+γmax⁡a′q∗(St+1,a′)∣St=s, At=a]\begin{aligned} q_*(s,a) = \mathbb{E}\Bigl[&R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a'} q_*(S_{t+1}, a') \\ &\Bigm| S_t = s,\, A_t = a\Bigr] \end{aligned} q∗​(s,a)=E[​Rt+1​+γa′max​q∗​(St+1​,a′)​St​=s,At​=a]​

Once you have q∗q_*q∗​, taking the action with the largest value in each state is an optimal policy, so solving the second equation solves the problem.

Derivation from the return
1. The return Eq. 3.8

Gt=Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2Rt+3+⋯=∑k=0∞γkRt+k+1\begin{aligned} G_t &= R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \cdots \\ &= \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k R_{t+k+1} \end{aligned} Gt​​=Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2Rt+3​+⋯=k=0∑∞​γkRt+k+1​​

2. Factor out γ Eq. 3.9

Gt=Rt+1+γ(Rt+2+γRt+3+⋯ )=Rt+1+γ Gt+1\begin{aligned} G_t &= R_{t+1} + \gamma\bigl(R_{t+2} + \gamma R_{t+3} + \cdots\bigr) \\ &= R_{t+1} + \gamma\, G_{t+1} \end{aligned} Gt​​=Rt+1​+γ(Rt+2​+γRt+3​+⋯)=Rt+1​+γGt+1​​

3. The episode ends at step T: nothing is left

GT=0G_T = 0 GT​=0

So the value of a terminal state is 0.

4. Values are expected returns Eq. 3.12 and 3.13

vπ(s)=Eπ ⁣[Gt∣St=s]qπ(s,a)=Eπ ⁣[Gt∣St=s, At=a]\begin{aligned} v_\pi(s) &= \mathbb{E}_\pi\!\left[G_t \mid S_t = s\right] \\ q_\pi(s,a) &= \mathbb{E}_\pi\!\left[G_t \mid S_t = s,\, A_t = a\right] \end{aligned} vπ​(s)qπ​(s,a)​=Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s]=Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s,At​=a]​

Putting equation 2 into equation 4 gives the Bellman equation for a policy. The value is not a new reward: Rt+1R_{t+1}Rt+1​ is real, and γ vπ(St+1)\gamma\, v_\pi(S_{t+1})γvπ​(St+1​) stands in for everything after it.

The deadly triad

Put three of these ideas together and the numbers can blow up: a formula in place of the table, a guess as the target, and off-policy learning, where the target describes a different rule from the one collecting the data. Sutton and Barto call it the deadly triad. DQN has all three, and uses replay and a frozen copy to reduce the instability. Part 5 shows how errors amplify.

Exact numbers: slot machines

Re-run of settings the game already uses, with its own RLA.run at commit 681cae3.

Ten machines with true averages drawn from a standard normal distribution, payout noise with standard deviation 1, 1,000 pulls, running averages (step size 1/n1/n1/n), 200 runs. Greedy starts all numbers at zero and breaks ties at random. Share of the last 200 pulls on the best machine, averaged over runs: greedy 35.5%, with random pulls 77.5%. Runs with less than half of the last 200 pulls on the best machine: 64.5% for greedy, 15.0% with random pulls. With random pulls, about 91% is the most possible, because one pull in ten is random.

The clip pair uses one run where greedy never pulled the best machine in its last 200 pulls and the other robot spent 92.5% there. I chose it because it shows the gap clearly. It is an example, not a typical run. Both robots share one set of machines.

How the clips were made

Each clip is a real recorded run drawn by a real browser with the game's own web/scenes.js at the same commit, unmodified. I replaced only the clock (30 frames per second) and encoded with ffmpeg (H.264). The run script and raw results are stored locally and are not published.
